newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Brazzaville truce holds, red tape blocks body hunt.
newsitem.headline: Brazzaville truce holds, red tape blocks body hunt.

text.p: A 72-hour truce held for a second successive day in the Congo Republic capital Brazzaville on Thursday but red tape thwarted Red Cross efforts to collect decomposing corpses that litter the city.

Former colonial power France, under pressure to leave some of its evacuation force in place until an intervention force can take over, said that it expected to have completed a planned withdrawal on schedule.
"If the entire operation goes as planned, (it) should be completed before Sunday," the Defence Ministry said in a statement in Paris.

The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), the only aid group at work in the city of a million people, said the truce had enabled them to bring the first help on Thursday to some of up to 1,500 badly wounded residents.

Barges plied the Congo river from Kinshasa in ex-Zaire to its twin city, laden with sanitation equipment to help aid workers remove the dead, some of whom have lain for days where they fell. Most were civilians caught in crossfire.
U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun, who visited Brazzaville on Wednesday on a mediation foray, said the sight of the corpses had sickened him.

But red tape prevented a swift start to an operation to rebury them. It should have got under way on Thursday after a green light from President Pascal Lissouba and his rival, former military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso.

"We have not been able to start yet. We have to coordinate through a ministerial committee for burial. There are medical-legal questions to be sorted out," ICRC spokesman Nick Sommer said in Kinshasa.

No one can yet tell how many people died in the fighting which began when Lissouba tried to disarm the "Cobras" militia of Sassou Nguesso, one of his main rivals in a presidential election that was to have been held on July 27.
The Red Cross said about 200 bodies were picked up in the first two days of the fighting, which has not spread to other parts of the oil-producing Central African nation.
The rest -- several hundred of them -- lie in central and northern parts of the city which basked in bright sunshine on Thursday for the first time in many days.
As the guns and artillery stayed silent, more people ventured out of the homes or other shelter, residents and officials said.

Some sneaked home across the frontlines from refuge in the peaceful Bacongo suburb, controlled by a third, neutral leader who has stayed out of the fray. "They have been fetching food from their freezers and homes and other belongings, then coming back to Bacongo," said one resident near to the centre of what was the colonial capital of French Equatorial Africa.
Government officials said vehicles were circulating again in the central swathe of Brazzaville that Lissouba still holds.

Other people from the ethnically mixed city are now refugees over in Kinshasa, an irony for the neighbouring capital which in May escaped its own bloody showdown when veteran president Mobutu Sese Seko fled Laurent Kabila's rebels.
More than 1,000 French troops plucked 5,700 foreigners out of Brazzaville.
